title: 3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
1.1 Option Pricing
Suppose we want to sell a European put with strike \(K\) and maturity \(T\). At maturity we would have to pay \[
(K-S_T)^+.
\] where \((S_t)_{t\geq 0}\) denotes the price process of the underlying stock. At which initial price should we sell our option?

title: 3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
1.2 Option Pricing via expected returns?
Idea 1 (Expected Return): Make the price a function of the expected return of the stock. However, one of the striking discoveries behind the Black–Scholes theory was that this expected return disappears from the option-pricing problem.

“The warrant value did not depend on the stock’s expected return … That fascinated me.”
— Fisher Black

title: 3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
1.3 Option Pricing via Replication
Idea 2: Replicate the option using the stock and the money-market account:

At \(t=0\), invest \(\Pi_0\)
at \(t\geq 0\), (re)balance the portfolio with value \(\Pi\) without external cash flows, investing

\[\Delta_t \text{ in the stock and the remaining } \Pi_t-\Delta_t S_t \text{ in the money-market account.}\]

at \(t=T\), the strategy should replicate the option’s payoff

\[
\Pi_T = (K-S_T)^+ \quad \text{a.s.}
\] If this is possible, no arbitrage implies \(\boxed{\text{Put price} = \Pi_0.}\)

1.3.1 Do such strategies exist?

title: 3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
1.4 Option Pricing via Replication (ctn.)
To get the idea, assume that the stock price follows a geometric Brownian motion (for simplicity) without a rate of return and zero intrerest rates, then the portfolio dynamics are \[d\Pi_t\overset{self-fin.}{=} \Delta_t dS_t\overset{.}{=} \Delta_t \sigma S_t dW_t.\] When the value process of the option is \(V(t,S_t)\) for a \(V\in C^{1,2}([0,T)\times \mathbb R)\), we find \[dV(t,S_t) \overset{\text{Ito's Lemma}}{=} \partial_t V(t,S_t) dt + \partial_s V(t,S_t) dS_t + \frac{\partial_{ss}V(t,S_t)}2 \sigma^2 S_t^2 dt\] Given the terminal condition \(V(T,S_T)= (K-S_T)^+\), this identifies \[
\begin{aligned}
&V,\text{ by comparing the drifts:}\,\boxed{\partial_t V(t,S_t) + \frac{\partial_{ss}V(t,S_t)}2 \sigma^2 S_t^2 = 0};\\
&\Delta,\text{ by comparing the volatilities}:\,\boxed{\Delta_t =  \partial_s V(t,S_t)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
2.1 Black Scholes Market
In the Black–Scholes model, the market is assumed to consist of two assets: a risky asset with price process \((S_t)_{t\geq 0}\) and the money-market account \((B_t)_{t\geq 0}\).
Since it is a riskless asset, the money-market account is assumed to grow at the risk-free rate \[
dB_t = r B_t\,dt,\qquad t\geq 0,
\quad \text{ so that
}\quad
B_t=B_0e^{rt}.
\]
The risky asset’s price is assumed to follow a geometric Brownian motion \[
dS_t = \mu S_t dt+\sigma S_t dW_t,
\quad \text{ so that
}\quad S_t = S_0 e^{\left(\mu-\frac{\sigma^2}2\right) t+\sigma W_t}\] where

\(\mu\in \mathbb R\) is the expected rate of return of the stock;
\(\sigma>0\) is its volatility;
\(W_t\) is a Brownian motion.

title: 3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
2.3 Self-financing Portfolios
Practically, a portfolio is self-financing, its value changes only because
1. the stock position changes in value; and 2. the cash position earns interest.
Formally, this leads to the following definition.






Definition (Self-financing Portfolio).
A portfolio with value process \((\Pi_t)_{t\geq 0}\) in the Black-Scholes market is called self-financing if its value satisfies \[
d\Pi_t
=
\Delta_t\,dS_t
+
r(\Pi_t-\Delta_tS_t)\,dt.
\]



The question is now whether we can choose \(\Delta_t\) in such a way that this self-financing portfolio exactly reproduces the payoff of the option.

title: 3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
3. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
3.2 Proof of the Black-Scholes formula
The value invested in the money-market account is \[
B_t=\Pi_t-\Delta_tS_t.
\]
Substituting the stock-price dynamics into the self-financing formula ?@eq-SFprop gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
d\Pi_t
&=
\Delta_t
\left(
\mu S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,dW_t
\right)
+
r(\Pi_t-\Delta_tS_t)\,dt
\\
&=
\left[
r\Pi_t
+
\Delta_t(\mu-r)S_t
\right]dt
+
\Delta_t\sigma S_t\,dW_t.
\end{aligned}
\]
Notice the three ingredients:

\(r\Pi_t\,dt\): the return the portfolio would earn at the risk-free rate;
\(\Delta_t(\mu-r)S_t\,dt\): the extra expected return obtained from holding the stock rather than cash;
\(\Delta_t\sigma S_t\,dW_t\): the random change caused by the stock-price shock.

The last term is the one that matters for hedging.
Let
\[
p(t,s)
\]
denote the value at time \(t\) of our European put when the stock price is \(s\).
The actual value of the put at time \(t\) is therefore the random variable
\[
P_t=p(t,S_t).
\]
At maturity there is no ambiguity about its value:
\[
p(T,s)=(K-s)^+.
\]
Before maturity, however, \(S_t\) is random, and hence \(p(t,S_t)\) is random.
We can determine how its value evolves using Itô’s formula. For a sufficiently smooth function \(p\),
\[
dp(t,S_t)
=
p_t(t,S_t)\,dt
+
p_s(t,S_t)\,dS_t
+
\frac12p_{ss}(t,S_t)(dS_t)^2.
\]
Because
\[
(dS_t)^2
=
\sigma^2S_t^2\,dt,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
dp(t,S_t)
&=
\left[
p_t
+
\mu S_t p_s
+
\frac12\sigma^2S_t^2p_{ss}
\right]dt
\\
&\qquad
+
\sigma S_t p_s\,dW_t,
\end{aligned}
\]
where, to keep the notation readable, all derivatives are evaluated at \((t,S_t)\).
Thus the option itself has a random \(dW_t\) term,
\[
\sigma S_t p_s\,dW_t.
\]
Compare this with the random term in the self-financing portfolio,
\[
\Delta_t\sigma S_t\,dW_t.
\]
This comparison contains the key idea.
We want the portfolio to reproduce the value of the option, i.e.
\[
\Pi_t=p(t,S_t).
\]
For this equality to persist after an infinitesimal stock-price movement, the two positions must have the same exposure to the Brownian shock \(dW_t\).
Therefore, assuming for the moment that \(p\) is differentiable in the price coordinate, we must choose
\[
\Delta_t=p_s(t,S_t).
\]
For a put, \(\Delta_t\) is negative. Intuitively, an increase in the stock price makes the right to sell the stock for \(K\) less valuable.
But matching the \(dW_t\) terms is only half the story. The deterministic \(dt\) terms must agree as well.
Using
\[
\Delta_t=p_s(t,S_t)
\]
in the portfolio equation gives
\[
d\Pi_t
=
\left[
r\Pi_t
+
(\mu-r)S_tp_s
\right]dt
+
\sigma S_tp_s\,dW_t.
\]
The option evolves according to
\[
dp(t,S_t)
=
\left[
p_t
+
\mu S_tp_s
+
\frac12\sigma^2S_t^2p_{ss}
\right]dt
+
\sigma S_tp_s\,dW_t.
\]
If \(\Pi_t=p(t,S_t)\), their drift terms must also be equal:
\[
rp
+
(\mu-r)S_tp_s
=
p_t
+
\mu S_tp_s
+
\frac12\sigma^2S_t^2p_{ss}.
\]
Now something remarkable happens.
The term involving the expected return \(\mu\) cancels. After rearranging,
\[
p_t(t,s)
+
rs\,p_s(t,s)
+
\frac12\sigma^2s^2p_{ss}(t,s)
=
rp(t,s).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
p_t
+
rs\,p_s
+
\frac12\sigma^2s^2p_{ss}
-rp
=
0.
\]
This is the Black–Scholes–Merton partial differential equation.

The expected return \(\mu\) of the stock has disappeared.

This is not because we assumed that \(\mu=r\). We did not.
It disappeared because the Delta hedge made the option and the replicating portfolio have exactly the same exposure to the random stock-price shock. Once that source of risk has been eliminated, no-arbitrage determines the remaining rate of return.
This answers the question with which we started the chapter.
We do not need to predict whether the stock is likely to rise or fall. We need to understand how strongly the option reacts when the stock moves and continuously adjust the stock position accordingly.
Suppose that we can find a function \(p(t,s)\) satisfying
\[
p_t
+
rs\,p_s
+
\frac12\sigma^2s^2p_{ss}
=
rp
\]
for \(0\leq t<T\), together with the terminal condition
\[
p(T,s)=(K-s)^+.
\]
Start with initial capital
\[
\Pi_0=p(0,S_0)
\]
and at every time use the strategy
\[
\Delta_t=p_s(t,S_t).
\]
The calculation above shows that the portfolio and the option then have identical infinitesimal changes:
\[
d\Pi_t=dp(t,S_t).
\]
Since they also have the same initial value,
\[
\Pi_t=p(t,S_t)
\]
for all \(t\).
In particular, at maturity,
\[
\Pi_T
=
p(T,S_T)
=
(K-S_T)^+.
\]
The terminal put payoff has therefore been replicated.
Under the assumptions of the model, this is not an approximation: it holds for every possible stock-price path.
Consequently,
\[
\text{option price}
=
\text{cost of the replicating portfolio}.
\]
Any other price would permit an arbitrage.
The stochastic problem has now become a deterministic one.
The Black–Scholes equation
\[
p_t
+
rs\,p_s
+
\frac12\sigma^2s^2p_{ss}
=
rp
\]
contains no Brownian motion and no expected stock return. Once the variables \(t\) and \(s\) are specified, it is simply a partial differential equation.
For a European option, the payoff at maturity provides the terminal condition.
For a call,
\[
c(T,s)=(s-K)^+,
\]
whereas for a put,
\[
p(T,s)=(K-s)^+.
\]
For the put it is also natural that
\[
p(t,s)\longrightarrow 0
\qquad\text{as }s\longrightarrow\infty,
\]
while if the stock price is zero,
\[
p(t,0)=Ke^{-r(T-t)}.
\]
The PDE together with these conditions determines the option value.
We will not derive the analytic PDE solution here. Instead, we state it and verify its implications.
Let
\[
\tau=T-t
\]
denote the time remaining until maturity and define
\[
d_1
=
\frac{
\ln(s/K)
+
\left(r+\frac12\sigma^2\right)\tau
}{
\sigma\sqrt{\tau}
},
\]
and
\[
d_2
=
d_1-\sigma\sqrt{\tau}
=
\frac{
\ln(s/K)
+
\left(r-\frac12\sigma^2\right)\tau
}{
\sigma\sqrt{\tau}
}.
\]
Let \(N\) denote the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal random variable.
Then the Black–Scholes value of a European call is
\[
c(t,s)
=
sN(d_1)
-
Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2).
\]
The European put price is
\[
p(t,s)
=
Ke^{-r\tau}N(-d_2)
-
sN(-d_1).
\]
We can now return to the rule used at the beginning of the chapter.
Differentiate the put price with respect to \(s\):
\[
\Delta_{\text{put}}
=
p_s(t,s).
\]
The result is
\[
\Delta_{\text{put}}
=
N(d_1)-1
=
-N(-d_1).
\]
Substituting the expression for \(d_1\) gives
\[
\Delta_{\text{put}}
=
N\!\left(
\frac{
\ln(s/K)
+
\left(r+\frac12\sigma^2\right)(T-t)
}{
\sigma\sqrt{T-t}
}
\right)-1.
\]
This is precisely the rule that we used at the beginning of the chapter.
It was not an arbitrary formula. It is the number of shares required by the replicating portfolio.
For a European put,
\[
-1<\Delta_{\text{put}}<0.
\]
Its interpretation is particularly clear in the limiting cases:

if the put is far out of the money, \(\Delta\) is close to \(0\);
if the put is far in the money, \(\Delta\) is close to \(-1\);
near the strike, Delta lies between these two extremes and changes rapidly as the stock moves.

Thus a put that is almost certain to expire in the money behaves approximately like a short position in one share of stock.

title: Computer-aided statistical analysis
text:
This is the course script for Computer-aided statistical analysis.
The course introduces essential ideas of modern applied and computational statistics, with particular emphasis on simulation experiments, regression modeling, model assessment, model selection, resampling, and cross-validation.
We will mostly study linear and generalized linear regression models, many of which you may already have encountered in earlier statistics courses. The distinguishing feature of this course is that computation is used systematically to investigate how statistical methods work, when approximations are accurate, how procedures behave in finite samples, and where their limitations become visible.
Throughout the course, we use Python and R as computational tools. In the lecture, examples will mostly be coded in Python.
The focus of this course is not on coding (So the Statistic part is much more important than the Computer part of the lecture). However, to follow the course, it is required, that you can at least understand an interpret the provided code.

title: Differential Equations with Financial Derivatives
section: Part I: Probability and stochastic calculus
text:
Part I: Probability and stochastic calculus
We begin with the probability theory and stochastic calculus required for continuous-time finance.
We study the concepts random variables and distributions, expectations, conditional expectations. We then introduce information structures, filtrations, and martingales and learn about Brownian motion, the stochastic integral and Itô’s formula, which is an invaluable tool in mathematical finance.

title: Differential Equations with Financial Derivatives
text:
Part II: Quantitative finance
The second part develops the foundations of continuous-time financial models. We start with the Black-Scholes formalism and will then study the theory of Arbitrage-free Pricing including the fundamental theorems of asset pricing. We will finally investigate the role of partial differential equations in financial mathematics in the context of local volatility models and give an outlook to modern methods in quantitative finance.

title: Computer-aided statistical analysis
section: Part I: Orientation and statistical foundations
text:
Part I: Orientation and statistical foundations
The course begins with an introductory week on the relationship between computation and statistics.
We briefly trace how increasing computational power changed statistical practice: from numerical calculation and simulation to resampling, computational optimization, and modern statistical learning. This provides the motivation for the central question of the course: how can computation help us understand, evaluate, and improve statistical methods?
The first Wednesday is a compact Python refresher. We review the computational tools needed for the rest of the course, including Jupyter notebooks, NumPy arrays, pandas data frames, functions, plotting, random-number generation, and reproducible use of random seeds. The aim is not to teach programming from scratch, but to establish a common computational workflow.
Weeks 2 and 3 then provide a compact refresher of probability and statistical inference.
We revisit random variables and distributions, expectations and moments, random samples, the law of large numbers, and the central limit theorem. We then move from populations to estimators and review sampling distributions, bias, variance, mean squared error, consistency, finite-sample distributions, and asymptotic distributions.
Simulation is integrated throughout this refresher. Rather than treating theoretical review and computational work as separate subjects, we use numerical experiments to examine how probability limits and asymptotic approximations appear in finite samples.
The third week ends with a complete Monte Carlo experiment. Students will formulate a data-generating process, identify an estimand and estimator, simulate repeated samples, estimate performance measures such as bias, variance, RMSE, and coverage, compare finite-sample results with theoretical or asymptotic approximations, and quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty.
The recurring perspective is:
[ . ]

title: Computer-aided statistical analysis
section: Part II: Linear models and model assessment
text:
Part II: Linear models and model assessment
Linear regression is our main laboratory for computer-aided statistical analysis.
We review simple and multiple linear regression and then focus on the aspects that become especially important in applied work: interpretation, prediction, categorical predictors, interactions, transformations, confidence and prediction intervals, and the distinction between explanatory and predictive goals.
Model specification and diagnostics are deliberately treated together. Residuals, leverage, influential observations, heteroskedasticity, and functional-form misspecification are studied both on real data and through deliberately constructed simulation experiments.
The part concludes by moving from in-sample fit to generalization. Training and test error, overfitting, the bias–variance trade-off, honest validation, and data leakage provide the conceptual basis for the model-selection and resampling methods that follow.

title: Computer-aided statistical analysis
section: Part III: Selection, resampling, and flexible regression
text:
Part III: Selection, resampling, and flexible regression
The third part asks how we should choose among competing models and how we should assess the uncertainty associated with that choice.
We study classical model-selection criteria and then devote the period around the Dies Academicus to cross-validation and resampling. Cross-validation is introduced on the Monday of CW 49 and developed further in CW 50 together with practical issues such as preprocessing, leakage, repeated validation, and the bootstrap.
We then move to regularization through ridge regression and the lasso. Particular attention is paid to the distinction between selecting a model, estimating its predictive performance, and quantifying uncertainty.
Finally, we relax the assumption of linearity in the predictors using polynomial regression, basis expansions, and splines.
Throughout this part, simulation studies are used to compare procedures under controlled data-generating mechanisms and to investigate questions that are difficult to answer from a single observed data set.

title: Computer-aided statistical analysis
section: Part IV: Generalized linear models and integration
text:
Part IV: Generalized linear models and integration
The fourth part extends the modeling framework to non-Gaussian response variables.
We introduce generalized linear models through logistic regression and then study the assessment of classification performance, including threshold-dependent measures, ROC ideas, calibration, and cross-validation.
Poisson regression provides a second important GLM example and allows us to revisit model diagnostics, dispersion, and simulation-based assessment in a different setting.
The final week combines the ideas of the course in an end-to-end analysis. The goal is not merely to fit a model, but to formulate a statistical question, construct a reproducible workflow, examine assumptions, compare alternatives, quantify predictive performance, understand uncertainty, and communicate the result.

title: 1. Random Variables, Distributions, and Limits
1. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
1.1 Sample spaces, Realizations and Events
The sample space \(\Omega\) is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment. An element \(\omega \in \Omega\) is called a realization (or outcome), while a subset \(A \subseteq \Omega\) is called an event.






NoteExamples




Coin toss (finite): We toss a coin once: \[\Omega = \{\text{Heads},\text{Tails}\}.\] An example of an event is \(A=\{\text{Heads}\}\).
Repeated coin tosses (countably infinite): We count the tosses until the first Heads: \[\Omega = \{1,2,3,\ldots\}.\] An example of an event is \(A=\{2,4,6,\ldots\}\).
Blood pressure (uncountable): We measure systolic blood pressure: \[\Omega = (0,\infty).\] An example of an event is \(A=[140,\infty)\).

title: 1. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
1.2 Probabilities
For a random experiment with sample space \(\Omega\), we will assign a probabilities, that is, a number \(\mathbb P[A]\) in \([0,1]\) to events \(A\subset \Omega\). The function \(\mathbb P[\cdot]\) is called a probability distribution or measure.






NoteDefinition: A function \(\mathbb P\) that assigns a number \(\mathbb P[A]\in [0,1]\) to an event \(A\) is a probability distribution, if it is




normalized, i.e. \(\mathbb P[\Omega]=1\) and
additive, that is, if \(A_1,A_2,...\) is a (potentially inifnite) sequence of events and these events are mutually disjoint, i.e. \(A_i\cap A_j =\emptyset\) when \(i\neq j\), then \[\mathbb P[\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}]= \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\mathbb P[A_i].\]









Warning



It is not always possible to assign a probability to each possible subset of a sample space, when the latter is uncountable. In this case, the distribution is defined only on a restricted family of subsets (a so-called \(\sigma\)-algebra).

title: 1. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
1.3 Interpretation of Probability
There are different interpretations for a probability \(\mathbb P[A]\). In this course, we will mostly concentrate on the *frequentist interpretation that tha \(\mathbb P[A]\) is the relative frequency of occurences of the event \(A\) after infinitely many independent repititions of the random experiment.

title: 1. The Black–Scholes Formalism
text:
1.4 Interpretation of Probability
In this course, we mainly use the frequentist interpretation:
\[
\mathbb P[A]
\]
is the relative frequency with which the event \(A\) occurs after many independent repetitions of the experiment.






NoteExamples



For a fair die, each number \(1,\dots,6\) should appear with relative frequency close to \[
\frac{1}{6}
\] when the number of repetitions becomes large.

title: 1. Random Variables, Distributions, and Limits
text:
1.1 Sample spaces, outcomes, and events
A random experiment has a sample space \(\Omega\), the set of possible outcomes. An event \(A\) is a subset of \(\Omega\) to which we can assign a probability.

A single coin toss: \(\Omega=\{H,T\}\), with event \(A=\{H\}\).
The number of tosses until the first heads: \(\Omega=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\).
Systolic blood pressure (continuous): We measure systolic blood pressure in mmHg, so \(\Omega=(0,\infty).\) An example of an event is (A=[140,)), indicating elevated blood pressure.

We describe probabilities by a probability distribution or measure \(\mathbb P\). A probability distribution is a function \(\mathbb P\) that assigns a number \(\mathbb P[A]\) in \([0,1]\) to an event \(A\subset \Omega\), and satisfies two conditions:

(normalization) \(\mathbb P[\Omega]=1\)
(countable additivity) for a (possibly infinite) number of events \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\), which are mutually disjoint, i.e. \(A_i\cap A_j = \emptyset\) when \(i\neq j\) it is \[
\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}A_i\right)
=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}\mathbb P(A_i).
\]







Warning



Strictly, probabilities are defined on a suitable collection of events (a \(\sigma\)-algebra), not necessarily on every subset of an uncountable sample space. We will usually leave the \(\sigma\)-algebra implicit.


Some useful consequences are summarized below: \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(\varnothing)&=0,\\
\mathbb P(A^c)&=1-\mathbb P(A),\\
A\subseteq B&\implies \mathbb P(A)\leq\mathbb P(B),\\
\mathbb P(A\cup B)&=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B).
\end{aligned}
\] Proof: On the blackboard
For \(\mathbb P(B)>0\), the conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is
\[
\mathbb P(A\mid B)=\frac{\mathbb P(A\cap B)}{\mathbb P(B)}.
\]
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if \(\mathbb P(A\cap B)=\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)\). Independence is not the same as being mutually exclusive.






ImportantFrequentist interpretation



In repeated independent trials with the same event probability \(p=\mathbb P(A)\), the observed fraction of trials in which \(A\) occurs tends toward \(p\) as the number of trials increases. This is a consequence of the law of large numbers, not an additional probability axiom.

title: 1. Random Variables, Distributions, and Limits
text:
1.2 A first experiment: relative frequencies
Simulate fair die rolls. The probability of each face is \(1/6\), but the empirical relative frequencies fluctuate from sample to sample.

rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=10_000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3.3), sharey=True)
for ax, n in zip(axes, [20, 200, 10_000]):
    frequencies = np.bincount(rolls[:n], minlength=7)[1:] / n
    ax.bar(np.arange(1, 7), frequencies)
    ax.axhline(1/6, color="black", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(f"n = {n:,}")
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(1, 7))
    ax.set_xlabel("Die face")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Relative frequency")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Relative frequencies of six die faces after different numbers of rolls. Dashed lines indicate the theoretical probability 1/6.











TipExercise 1



Consider two events with \(\mathbb P(A)=0.4\), \(\mathbb P(B)=0.5\), and \(\mathbb P(A\cap B)=0.2\). Calculate \(\mathbb P(A\cup B)\) and \(\mathbb P(A\mid B)\). Are \(A\) and \(B\) independent? What would change if they were disjoint?

title: 1. Random Variables, Distributions, and Limits
text:
1.3 Random variables
A (real-valued) random variable is a (measurable) function \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb R\). It assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment. Its distribution tells us which values it takes and with what probabilities. For example, if \(X\) indicates whether a coin toss gives heads, then \(X=1\) for heads and \(X=0\) for tails.
The distinction is important: \(X\) is a random variable, \(x\) is a possible value, and \(X(\omega)\) is its realized value for a particular outcome \(\omega\).
In practice, we often do not know—or care about—the full sample space \(\Omega\). It may represent all possible states of the world, including many details that we cannot observe. A random variable allows us to focus on one particular feature of this complexity.
For example, the outcome of a coin toss depends on many physical factors: the force of the flip, the angle, air resistance, and so on. Rather than modeling all these details, we define \(X=1\) if the coin lands heads and \(X=0\) otherwise. Assuming a fair coin, we simply write \[
\mathbb P[X=1]=\mathbb P[\{\omega \in \Omega: X(\omega)=0\}]=\frac12.
\]
More generally, the distribution of \(X\) describes the probabilities of the values we actually observe, without requiring us to model everything that produces them: \[

\]

title: 1. Random Variables, Distributions, and Limits
text:
7.3 Conditional Probability and Conditional Expectation
In many statistical applications, we want to make predictions about a random variable \(Y\) based on information about another random variable \(X\) For example, we might want to predict a person’s income from their education, or the probability of developing a disease from age and other characteristics.
The mathematical concepts underlying these questions are conditional probability and conditional expectation.

7.3.1 Discrete Case
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are discrete random variables, we write \[\begin{align*}
\mathbb P[Y=y\mid X=x]
= &
\frac{\mathbb P[Y=y,X=x]}{\mathbb P[X=x]},\\
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]
= &
\sum_y y\,\mathbb P[Y=y\mid X=x],
\end{align*}\] for conditional probabilities and conditional expectations, provided \(\mathbb P[X=x]>0\), assuming the sum is absolutely convergent.
In particular, for each possible value \(x\), we obtain a number \[
m(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x].
\] The function \(m\) is called the conditional expectation function or regression function.
The random variable \(m(X)\) is denoted by \(\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\).






NoteExample: Two dice



We roll two independent fair dice. Let \(X\) denote the result of the first die and \(Y\) the sum of both dice.
Then
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=x+3.5.
\]
Hence, knowing the outcome of the first die changes our expected value of the sum.


Conditional expectations satisfy several useful properties.






Note



Lemma:(Properties of conditional expectations)
Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable and let \(Y,Z\) be integrable random variables.

Linearity:
\[
\mathbb E[aY+bZ\mid X]
=
a\mathbb E[Y\mid X]+b\mathbb E[Z\mid X].
\]
Taking out what is known: For a function \(h\),
\[
\mathbb E[h(X)Y\mid X]
=
h(X)\mathbb E[Y\mid X],
\]
provided the quantities are integrable. In particular,
\[
\mathbb E[h(X)\mid X]=h(X).
\]
Law of iterated expectations:
\[
\mathbb E[\mathbb E[Y\mid X]]
=
\mathbb E[Y].
\]



Proof: On the blackboard, using the definition for discrete random variables.






TipFinger exercise



Show that if \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, then
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X]=\mathbb E[Y].
\]


The conditional expectation has a particularly useful property: it is the best predictor of \(Y\) based on \(X\) when prediction errors are measured by mean squared error.
To see this, let
\[
m(X)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X].
\]
For any function \(g\), assuming finite second moments, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2\mid X]
&=\mathbb E[(Y-m(X)+m(X)-g(X))^2\mid X]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))^2\mid X]\\
&\quad+2(m(X)-g(X))
\underbrace{\mathbb E[Y-m(X)\mid X]}_{=0}\\
&\quad+(m(X)-g(X))^2\\
&\geq \mathbb E[(Y-m(X))^2\mid X].
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking expectations on both sides gives
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2]
\geq
\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))^2].
}
\]
Thus, \(m(X)\) minimizes the mean squared prediction error among all square-integrable functions of \(X\).


7.3.2 Continuous case
In regression, we often want to calculate expressions such as \[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x],
\] where \(X\) has a density. But then \(\mathbb P[X=x]=0\) for every \(x\). Consequently, the definition based on dividing by \(\mathbb P[X=x]\) does not work.

How can we define conditional expectations in this situation?

The answer is surprisingly simple: We can directly define the conditional expectation function \(m\) as the function that optimally predicts \(Y\) from \(X\) in mean square.
That is, if \(\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty\), the conditional expectation \(m(X)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\) satisfies \[
\boxed{
m\in\underset{g}{\operatorname{argmin}}\;
\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2].
}
\]






Note




the minimum is not taken over all functions \(g\), but over all functions, for which the expectation \(E[(Y-g(X))^2]\) is well-defined. This class is very large and the corresponding functions are called measurable functions.
Strictly, the minimizing random variable \(m(X)\) is unique up to almost-sure equality. Accordingly, \(m(x)\) is determined only for \(P_X\)-almost every \(x\).









Tip



There are other, equivalent characterizations of conditional expectation. For instance, when a conditional density exists, \[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
y f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\,dy.
\] See Wasserman (2004), All of Statistics, Section 3.5, for conditional expectations defined through conditional distributions.
The least-squares characterization is particularly useful for regression because it does not require us to calculate conditional densities explicitly.


Remarkably, the properties established for discrete \(X\), including linearity, taking out what is known, and the law of iterated expectations, also hold for general random variables, provided the relevant expectations exist.
There are some interesting consequences of our definition. First, Prediction errors have conditional mean zero. That is, \[
\varepsilon:=Y-\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\Rightarrow
\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X]=0.
\]
Second, the law of total variance holds, that is, for a square-integrable random variable \(Y\), \[
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]
+
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[Y\mid X]).
\] The first term describes the variability remaining after observing \(X\). The second describes the variability of the conditional expectation.
Proof: Finger exercise. Use the law of iterated expectations and the decomposition
\[
Y-\mathbb E[Y]
=
(Y-\mathbb E[Y\mid X])
+
(\mathbb E[Y\mid X]-\mathbb E[Y]).
\]


7.3.3 Conditional probabilities as conditional expectations
There is an important connection between conditional probabilities and conditional expectations.
For an event \(A\), let \(\mathbf 1_A\) be its indicator variable, equal to 1 when \(A\) occurs and 0 otherwise.
Then
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P[A\mid X]
=
\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A\mid X].
}
\]
In particular, if \(Y\in\{0,1\}\) is a binary random variable,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]
=
\mathbb P[Y=1\mid X=x].
}
\]
This identity will become central when we study logistic regression, where our goal is to model the conditional probability of a binary outcome.






TipFinger exercise



Let \(Y\in\{0,1\}\).

Show that \(\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb P[Y=1]\).
Explain why \(\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=\mathbb P[Y=1\mid X=x]\).
Show that
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)
=
p(X)(1-p(X)),
\]
where \(p(X)=\mathbb P[Y=1\mid X]\).

5.3 Simulation laboratory: Conditional expectation and prediction
We investigate how conditional expectations help us predict a random variable.
Suppose that
\[
X\sim N(0,1),\qquad Y=X^2+\varepsilon,
\]
where \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,1)\) is independent of \(X\).
Since \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X]=0\),
\[
m(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=x^2.
\]
We consider three predictors:
\[
g_1(x)=1,\qquad g_2(x)=x,\qquad g_3(x)=x^2.
\]

5.3.1 Experiment 1: Visualizing conditional expectations

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

n = 1000
x = rng.normal(size=n)
epsilon = rng.normal(size=n)
y = x**2 + epsilon

grid = np.linspace(-3, 3, 300)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))

ax.scatter(x, y, alpha=0.25, s=12, label="Observations")
ax.plot(grid, grid**2, linewidth=2.5,
        label="Conditional expectation")
ax.plot(grid, np.ones_like(grid), linestyle="--",
        label="Unconditional expectation")

ax.set_xlabel("X")
ax.set_ylabel("Y")
ax.legend()
plt.show()










5.3.2 Experiment 2: Comparing prediction errors
We compare the mean squared prediction errors of the three prediction functions.

predictions = {
    "Constant": np.ones(n),
    "Linear": x,
    "Conditional expectation": x**2
}

for name, prediction in predictions.items():
    mse = np.mean((y - prediction)**2)
    print(f"{name:25s}: MSE = {mse:.3f}")

Constant                 : MSE = 2.988
Linear                   : MSE = 5.026
Conditional expectation  : MSE = 1.035




5.3.3 Experiment 3: Monte Carlo approximation
Now repeat the experiment many times and investigate how close the simulated MSEs are to their theoretical values.

R = 1000
n = 100

mse = np.empty((R, 3))

for r in range(R):
    x = rng.normal(size=n)
    epsilon = rng.normal(size=n)
    y = x**2 + epsilon

    mse[r, 0] = np.mean((y - 1)**2)
    mse[r, 1] = np.mean((y - x)**2)
    mse[r, 2] = np.mean((y - x**2)**2)

print("Average MSE across replications:")
print(mse.mean(axis=0))

print("Theoretical MSE:")
print([3, 5, 1])

Average MSE across replications:
[3.047313   5.0269604  1.01022953]
Theoretical MSE:
[3, 5, 1]








TipExercises




Show analytically that \[
\mathbb E[Y]=1,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.
\]
Calculate the theoretical mean squared prediction errors of \(g_1\), \(g_2\), and \(g_3\).
Explain why \(g_3\) is the best predictor, even though individual observations may lie far away from the curve \(y=x^2\).
Change the sample size \(n\). How does the variability of the simulated MSE change?
Replace \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,1)\) with \(\varepsilon\sim N(0,4)\). How does the conditional expectation change? How do the mean squared prediction errors change?
Explain why the fact that \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0\) does not imply that \(X\) is useless for predicting \(Y\).

\begin{aligned}

\end{aligned}

\boxed{
\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2]
\geq
\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))^2].

text:
3.2 General case
In regression, we often want to calculate expressions such as \[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x],
\] where \(X\) has a density. But then \(\mathbb P[X=x]=0\) for every \(x\). Consequently, the definition based on dividing by \(\mathbb P[X=x]\) does not work.

How can we define conditional expectations in this situation?

The answer is surprisingly simple: We can directly define the conditional expectation function \(m\) as the function that optimally predicts \(Y\) from \(X\) in mean square. That is, if \(\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty\), the conditional expectation \(m(X)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\) satisfies \[
\boxed{
m\in\underset{g}{\operatorname{argmin}}\;
\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2].
}
\]






Note




the minimum is not taken over all functions \(g\), but over all functions, for which the expectation \(E[(Y-g(X))^2]\) is well-defined. This class is very large and the corresponding functions are called measurable functions.
Strictly, the minimizing random variable \(m(X)\) is unique up to almost-sure equality. Accordingly, \(m(x)\) is determined only for \(P_X\)-almost every \(x\).









Tip



There are other, equivalent characterizations of conditional expectation. For instance, when a conditional density exists, \[
\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]
=
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
y f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\,dy.
\] See Wasserman (2004), All of Statistics, Section 3.5, for conditional expectations defined through conditional distributions.
The least-squares characterization is particularly useful for regression because it does not require us to calculate conditional densities explicitly.


We may also define more general conditional moments. Of particular importance is the conditional variance which describes the remaining variability of \(Y\) when \(X\) is known, that is, for a square-integrable random variable \(Y\), the conditional variance of \(Y\) given \(X\) is \[
\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)
=
\mathbb E\left[
(Y-\mathbb E[Y\mid X])^2\mid X
\right].
\] Equivalently, \[
\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)
=
\mathbb E[Y^2\mid X]
-
(\mathbb E[Y\mid X])^2.
\]

3.2.1 Properties of conditional expectation and variance
Conditional Expectations have many desirable properties.






NoteLemma: Properties of conditional expectations



Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables with \(\mathbb E[Y^2]<\infty\), and write \(m(X)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\).
The following properties hold:

Centered residuals and orthogonality:
\[
\mathbb E[Y-m(X)\mid X]=0,
\]
and, for every square-integrable function \(h(X)\),
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))h(X)]=0.
\]
Linearity: For square-integrable random variables \(Y,Z\),
\[
\mathbb E[aY+bZ\mid X]
=a\mathbb E[Y\mid X]+b\mathbb E[Z\mid X].
\]
Taking out what is known: For a bounded measurable function \(h\),
\[
\mathbb E[h(X)Y\mid X]
=h(X)\mathbb E[Y\mid X].
\]
In particular,
\[
\mathbb E[h(X)\mid X]=h(X).
\]
Law of iterated expectations (tower property):
\[
\mathbb E[\mathbb E[Y\mid X]]=\mathbb E[Y].
\]
Law of total variance:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]
+
\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[Y\mid X]),
\]
where
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)
=
\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))^2\mid X].
\]

All equalities between conditional expectations hold almost surely.


Proof. We use the characterization of conditional expectation as the minimizer of mean squared prediction error.
1. Orthogonality. Since \(m(X)\) minimizes \(\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2]\), for every square-integrable \(h(X)\), the function
\[
q(t)=\mathbb E[(Y-m(X)-th(X))^2]
\]
is minimized at \(t=0\). Differentiating gives
\[
q'(0)=-2\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))h(X)]=0.
\]
Thus,
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))h(X)]=0.
\]
In particular, the conditional expectation of the residual \(Y-m(X)\) is zero, since the zero function is its best mean squared predictor based on \(X\).
2. Linearity. Write \(m_Y(X)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\) and \(m_Z(X)=\mathbb E[Z\mid X]\). For every square-integrable \(h(X)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E[(aY+bZ-am_Y(X)-bm_Z(X))h(X)]\\
&=a\mathbb E[(Y-m_Y(X))h(X)]\\
&\quad+b\mathbb E[(Z-m_Z(X))h(X)]=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence \(am_Y(X)+bm_Z(X)\) is the best mean squared predictor of \(aY+bZ\) based on \(X\).
3. Taking out what is known. For bounded \(h(X)\) and every square-integrable function \(g(X)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E[(h(X)Y-h(X)m(X))g(X)]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))h(X)g(X)]=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(h(X)m(X)\) is the best mean squared predictor of \(h(X)Y\). Moreover, if \(Y=h(X)\), then \(Y\) can be predicted perfectly from \(X\), so \(\mathbb E[h(X)\mid X]=h(X)\) (for any square-integrable \(h(X)\)).
4. Law of iterated expectations. Choosing \(h(X)=1\) in the orthogonality property gives
\[
\mathbb E[Y-m(X)]=0,
\]
which proves the claim.
5. Law of total variance. Write
\[
Y-\mathbb E[Y]
=
(Y-m(X))+(m(X)-\mathbb E[Y]).
\]
Squaring and taking expectations, the cross term vanishes by orthogonality. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
&=\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))^2]\\
&\quad+\mathbb E[(m(X)-\mathbb E[Y])^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]
+\operatorname{Var}(m(X)),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the final equality uses the law of iterated expectations. \(\square\)


3.2.2 Conditional Probabilities in the continuous case
We may also define conditional probabilities in the context of continuous random variables via conditional expectations. For an event \(A\), let \[
\mathbf 1_A(\omega):=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \omega \in A\\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\] be its indicator variable. Then \[
\boxed{
\mathbb P[A\mid X]
=
\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A\mid X].
}
\]

text:
8.4 Looking ahead
We know that a sample mean varies from sample to sample and can often be approximated by a Normal distribution. In Chapter 2 we will treat such sample summaries as estimators, assess their bias, variance and mean squared error, introduce consistency and asymptotic normality, and plan a complete Monte Carlo experiment with appropriate measures of simulation uncertainty. :::

title: 1. Random Variables, Distributions, and Limits
text:
2.1 Convergence of random variables
When studying the empirical mean \(\overline X_n\), we want to understand what happens as the sample size \(n\) increases. Unlike a sequence of ordinary numbers, however, \(\overline X_n\) is a random variable for every \(n\): its value depends on the particular sample we draw.
What does it mean for a sequence of random variables \(Y_1,Y_2,\ldots\) to converge to some random variable \(Y\)? There are several answers, depending on what exactly we require to become close. We recall four important notions.

2.1.1 Convergence in probability
We say that \(Y_n\) converges in probability to \(Y\), written
\[
Y_n\xrightarrow{P}Y,
\]
if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\mathbb P(|Y_n-Y|>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow 0
\qquad (n\to\infty).
\]
Intuition: For a sufficiently large \(n\), it becomes increasingly unlikely that \(Y_n\) differs substantially from \(Y\).
For example, if \(Y_n=\overline X_n\) and \(Y=\mu\) is the population mean, convergence in probability means that the sample average is increasingly likely to be close to the true mean. This is precisely the conclusion of the weak law of large numbers.
Importantly, convergence in probability does not require that every possible sequence of realized values eventually stays close to the limit. Large deviations can still occur, but their probabilities vanish.


2.1.2 Almost sure convergence
We say that \(Y_n\) converges almost surely to \(Y\), written
\[
Y_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}Y,
\]
if
\[
\mathbb P\left(
\left\{\omega\in\Omega:
\lim_{n\to\infty}Y_n(\omega)=Y(\omega)
\right\}
\right)=1.
\]
Intuition: Imagine repeatedly extending the same sequence of observations. Almost sure convergence means that, with probability one, the resulting sequence of values eventually stays arbitrarily close to its limit.
The difference from convergence in probability is subtle but important:

In probability: At each large \(n\), the probability of a substantial deviation is small.
Almost surely: Along almost every individual infinite sequence of outcomes, substantial deviations eventually stop occurring.

Almost sure convergence is therefore stronger than convergence in probability. The strong law of large numbers establishes this stronger property for sample averages.


2.1.3 Convergence in mean square
We say that \(Y_n\) converges in mean square (or in \(L^2\)) to \(Y\), written
\[
Y_n\xrightarrow{L^2}Y,
\]
if
\[
\mathbb E[(Y_n-Y)^2]\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Intuition: The expected squared error between \(Y_n\) and \(Y\) vanishes.
For sample averages of i.i.d. observations with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\), we have by Bienaymé’s formula \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(\overline X_n-\mu)^2]
=  \operatorname{Var}(\overline X_n)
= & \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}( X_i)}{n^2}\\
= & \frac{\sigma^2}{n}
\longrightarrow 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, the empirical mean converges in mean square to the population mean. This also provides a particularly transparent reason why larger samples tend to produce more precise averages.
Mean-square convergence implies convergence in probability, as follows directly from Markov’s inequality applied to \((Y_n-Y)^2\):
\[
\mathbb P(|Y_n-Y|>\varepsilon)
\leq
\frac{\mathbb E[(Y_n-Y)^2]}{\varepsilon^2}
\longrightarrow 0.
\]


2.1.4 Convergence in distribution
Finally, we say that \(Y_n\) converges in distribution to \(Y\), written
\[
Y_n\xrightarrow{d}Y,
\]
if their cumulative distribution functions satisfy
\[
F_{Y_n}(t)\longrightarrow F_Y(t)
\]
at every point \(t\) where \(F_Y\) is continuous.
Intuition: The probability distribution of \(Y_n\) increasingly resembles the distribution of \(Y\). We do not require the individual values of \(Y_n\) and \(Y\) to be close.
For example, suppose that \(Y_n\) and \(Y\) are independent standard normal random variables for every \(n\). Their distributions are identical, so trivially
\[
Y_n\xrightarrow{d}Y.
\]
However, \(Y_n\) does not converge in probability to \(Y\): even for large \(n\), two independently drawn standard normal values can differ substantially.
Convergence in distribution is particularly important for the central limit theorem. The CLT does not say that sample averages themselves converge to a normally distributed random variable. Instead, it says that the distribution of appropriately standardized sample averages approaches a normal distribution.


2.1.5 How are these notions related?
The four convergence concepts form the following hierarchy:
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}Y
&\implies Y_n\xrightarrow{P}Y,\\[4pt]
Y_n\xrightarrow{L^2}Y
&\implies Y_n\xrightarrow{P}Y,\\[4pt]
Y_n\xrightarrow{P}Y
&\implies Y_n\xrightarrow{d}Y.
\end{aligned}
\]
Almost sure convergence and mean-square convergence do not, in general, imply one another.
Most reverse implications are false. Two simple examples illustrate why.


2.1.6 Counterexamples: Why the notions of convergence matter
The implications between the different types of convergence generally cannot be reversed. Two examples illustrate why.

2.1.6.1 Counterexample 1: Convergence in probability does not imply convergence in mean square
Consider the random variables
\[
Y_n =
\begin{cases}
n, & \text{with probability }1/n^2,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\) and sufficiently large \(n\),
\[
\mathbb P(|Y_n|>\varepsilon)=\frac{1}{n^2}\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Thus, \(Y_n\xrightarrow{P}0\). However,
\[
\mathbb E[Y_n^2]=n^2\cdot\frac{1}{n^2}=1
\]
for every \(n\), so \(Y_n\) does not converge in mean square to zero.
Intuition: Very large values become increasingly rare, but their squared magnitude grows fast enough to keep the expected squared error constant.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3.2))

for ax, n in zip(axes, [2, 5, 10]):
    probabilities = [1 - 1/n**2, 1/n**2]
    ax.bar([0, 1], probabilities, color=["steelblue", "darkorange"])
    ax.set_xticks([0, 1], ["0", str(n)])
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
    ax.set_title(f"n = {n}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Value of $Y_n$")
    ax.text(1, probabilities[1] + 0.04,
            f"{1/n**2:.2%}", ha="center", fontsize=9)

axes[0].set_ylabel("Probability")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 3: Rare but increasingly large deviations. The nonzero value grows with n, while its probability shrinks.







2.1.6.2 Counterexample 2: Convergence in probability does not imply almost sure convergence
Consider the sample space \(\Omega=[0,1)\) with the uniform distribution. We construct a sequence of random variables that equal \(1\) on a small interval and \(0\) elsewhere.
First, we select the entire interval \([0,1)\). Next, we select its two halves in turn, then its four quarters, then its eight eighths, and so on.
More precisely, for \(n=2^k+j\), with \(k\geq 0\) and \(j=0,\ldots,2^k-1\), define
\[
Y_n(\omega)=
\begin{cases}
1, & \displaystyle \omega\in
\left[\frac{j}{2^k},\frac{j+1}{2^k}\right),\\[6pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The following diagram illustrates this construction. Each colored interval represents the set of outcomes for which \(Y_n=1\).

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))

omega = 0.3
rows = []

for k in range(4):
    for j in range(2**k):
        rows.append((k, j, j / 2**k, (j+1) / 2**k))

for i, (k, j, left, right) in enumerate(rows):
    ax.barh(i, right-left, left=left, height=0.75,
            color="steelblue", edgecolor="white")

ax.axvline(omega, color="darkorange", ls="--", lw=2,
           label=rf"Fixed outcome $\omega={omega}$")

ax.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylim(len(rows)-0.2, -0.8)
ax.set_xlabel(r"Outcome $\omega\in[0,1)$")
ax.set_ylabel("Random variable $Y_n$")

ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)))
ax.set_yticklabels([f"$Y_{{{i+1}}}$" for i in range(len(rows))])

ax.legend(loc="lower right")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 4: The typewriter sequence. At each stage, a smaller interval moves from left to right across the sample space. The dashed line indicates a fixed outcome.





Convergence in probability: At stage \(k\), the interval where \(Y_n=1\) has length \(2^{-k}\). Hence,
\[
\mathbb P(Y_n=1)=2^{-k}\longrightarrow 0
\]
as \(n\to\infty\). Therefore, \(Y_n\xrightarrow{P}0\).
Almost sure convergence: Fix any \(\omega\in[0,1)\). At every stage \(k\), exactly one of the intervals contains \(\omega\). Thus, \(Y_n(\omega)=1\) infinitely often. It also equals \(0\) infinitely often.
Consequently, \(Y_n(\omega)\) does not converge for any \(\omega\in[0,1)\), and almost sure convergence fails.
Intuition: The interval where \(Y_n=1\) becomes smaller and smaller, but keeps moving across the sample space. Deviations become increasingly unlikely at each step, yet every individual outcome is hit infinitely often.






ImportantKey takeaway




Convergence in probability: The probability of a substantial deviation becomes arbitrarily small.
Almost sure convergence: Along almost every individual sequence of outcomes, substantial deviations eventually stop occurring.
Convergence in mean square: The expected squared error becomes arbitrarily small.

These requirements are different, and convergence in probability alone does not guarantee either of the other two.

text:
2.2 Law of large numbers
The law of large numbers (LLN) formalizes a fundamental idea in statistics: averages of repeated random observations approach their theoretical expectations as the sample size increases.
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be i.i.d. observations with \(\mathbb E[|X_1|]<\infty\) and mean \(\mu=\mathbb E[X_1]\). The weak law of large numbers states that
\[
\boxed{
\overline X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
\xrightarrow{P}\mu.
}
\]
Thus, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
\mathbb P(|\overline X_n-\mu|\geq\varepsilon)
\longrightarrow 0.
\]
The strong LLN establishes the stronger result \(\overline X_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mu\): along almost every infinite sequence of observations, the sample average approaches \(\mu\).
If \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty\), we have seen, that the empirical mean converges in mean square by Markov’s, which is implies the weak law of large numbers. Precisely, we have seen that: \[
\mathbb P(|\overline X_n-\mu|\geq\varepsilon)
\leq \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}
\longrightarrow 0.
\] This establishes convergence, although the bound may be much larger than the actual deviation probability.

2.2.1 Frequentist interpretation: probabilities and moments
The LLN connects theoretical properties of a distribution to observable quantities in repeated experiments.
Indeed, we can apply it to any function \(g(X)\) with finite absolute expectation:
\[
\boxed{
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(X_i)
\xrightarrow{a.s.}\mathbb E[g(X)].
}
\]
Two important applications are:

Probabilities: For \(g(X)=\mathbf 1\{X\in A\}\), the observed relative frequency of an event approaches its probability \(\mathbb P(X\in A)\).
Moments: For \(g(X)=X^k\), the empirical moment \(n^{-1}\sum_i X_i^k\) approaches the theoretical moment \(\mathbb E[X^k]\), provided \(\mathbb E[|X|^k]<\infty\).

This provides the frequentist interpretation of probabilities and moments discussed earlier.
Consider \(X_i\sim\mathrm{Exponential}(1)\). We know that
\[
\mathbb P(X_i\leq 1)=1-e^{-1},
\qquad
\mathbb E[X_i^k]=k!.
\]
We compare empirical event frequencies with empirical moments as the sample size increases.

from math import factorial

rng_lln = np.random.default_rng(2026)
N = 30_000
n = np.arange(1, N + 1)
samples = rng_lln.exponential(size=(3, N))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))

# Event probabilities: three independent sample paths
p = 1 - np.exp(-1)

for x in samples:
    freq = np.cumsum(x <= 1) / n
    axes[0].plot(n, freq, lw=1, alpha=0.8)

axes[0].axhline(p, color="black", ls="--", label=r"$P(X\leq 1)$")
axes[0].set_title("Relative frequency")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"Fraction with $X_i\leq 1$")
axes[0].legend()

# Empirical moments: same observations, different powers
x = samples[0]

for k in [1, 2, 4]:
    empirical = np.cumsum(x**k) / n
    axes[1].plot(n, empirical / factorial(k), lw=1,
                 label=fr"$k={k}$")

axes[1].axhline(1, color="black", ls="--")
axes[1].set_title("Empirical moments")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Empirical / theoretical moment")
axes[1].legend()

for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_xlim(100, N)
    ax.set_xlabel("Sample size $n$")

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 5: Law of large numbers: empirical event frequencies (left) and normalized empirical moments (right) from Exponential(1) observations. Dashed lines indicate population values.





What do we observe?
Both relative frequencies and empirical moments approach their theoretical values. However, higher empirical moments fluctuate more strongly and may require considerably larger samples to become precise.
The reason is their variance. If \(\mathbb E[X^{2k}]<\infty\),
\[
\operatorname{Var}\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^k
\right)
=
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X^k)}{n}.
\]
For our Exponential(1) example,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X^k)=(2k)!-(k!)^2.
\]
Consequently, the relative standard errors of the first, second, and fourth empirical moments are
\[
\frac{1}{\sqrt n},\qquad
\frac{\sqrt 5}{\sqrt n},\qquad
\frac{\sqrt{69}}{\sqrt n},
\]
respectively.
All three estimators converge, but the higher moments are much less precise for a given sample size.
Consequently, the LLN tells us that empirical averages converge to their theoretical expectations. Markov’s inequality provides an upper bound on their deviation probabilities. But neither tells us precisely how likely a given estimation error is in a finite sample.
To understand the distribution of these errors, rather than merely bound their probabilities, we turn to the central limit theorem.

title: 1. Random Variables, Distributions, and Limits
text:
2.3 Central limit theorem
The LLN establishes that empirical averages converge to their theoretical expectations. But how precise is an empirical average for a given sample size? Markov’s inequality provides an upper bound on the probability of an estimation error, but this bound can be very conservative. The central limit theorem (CLT) provides a more informative answer by approximating the sampling distribution of empirical averages.
For i.i.d. observations with \(\mathbb E[X_i]=\mu\) and \(0<\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty\), \[
\boxed{
\frac{\sqrt n(\overline X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}
\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).
}
\]
Recall that convergence in distribution means that the CDFs converge at every continuity point of the limiting CDF. Thus, for sufficiently large \(n\), the sample mean is approximately Normally distributed: \[
\overline X_n\ \overset{\text{approx.}}\sim\
N\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
\] The LLN tells us where the sample mean concentrates. The CLT describes the distribution of its fluctuations around the population mean.
Let \(\Phi\) denote the CDF of the standard Normal distribution. The CLT suggests that, for sufficiently large \(n\), \[
\mathbb P\left(
|\overline X_n-\mu|\geq z\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
\right)
\approx 2[1-\Phi(z)].
\] For example, consider deviations larger than two standard errors:

Markov’s inequality: The probability is at most \(1/4=25\%\).
CLT approximation: The probability is approximately \(4.6\%\).

Unlike Markov’s inequality, the CLT provides an approximation rather than a guaranteed bound. Its accuracy depends on the population distribution and the sample size.

2.3.1 Frequentist interpretation: Centered Moments as uncertainty indicators
As with the LLN, we can apply the CLT to any transformation \(g(X)\) with finite, positive variance: \[
\frac{
\sqrt n\left(
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n g(X_i)-\mathbb E[g(X)]
\right)
}{
\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(g(X))}
}
\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1).
\]
In particular, choosing \(g(X)=X^k\) gives a Normal approximation for empirical moments, provided \(\mathbb E[X^{2k}]<\infty\).
Recall our Exponential(1) example:
\[
\mathbb E[X^k]=k!,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X^k)=(2k)!-(k!)^2.
\]
Higher empirical moments have much larger relative standard errors. Moreover, the distributions of \(X^k\) become increasingly skewed, so their Normal approximations may require much larger sample sizes to become accurate.
We return to \(X_i\sim\mathrm{Exponential}(1)\) and simulate many independent samples. We compare the standardized empirical mean and fourth empirical moment with the standard Normal density.

from math import factorial

rng_clt = np.random.default_rng(2027)
R = 10_000
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3.5))

grid = np.linspace(-3.5, 3.5, 300)
bins = np.linspace(-3.5, 3.5, 71)
bin_width = bins[1] - bins[0]

for ax, (k, n) in zip(axes, [(1, 5), (1, 40), (4, 40)]):

    samples = rng_clt.exponential(size=(R, n))
    mu_k = factorial(k)
    sigma_k = np.sqrt(factorial(2*k) - mu_k**2)

    empirical = np.mean(samples**k, axis=1)
    z = np.sqrt(n) * (empirical - mu_k) / sigma_k

    # Fixed bin weights: excluded tails are not renormalized
    ax.hist(z, bins=bins,
            weights=np.full(R, 1 / (R * bin_width)),
            alpha=0.7, color="steelblue")
    ax.plot(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid), "k--", lw=1.5)

    ax.set_title(fr"Moment $k={k}$, $n={n}$")
    ax.set_xlabel("Standardized error")
    ax.set_xlim(-3.5, 3.5)

    if k == 1 and n == 40:
        deviation_frequency = np.mean(np.abs(z) >= 2)

axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Simulated deviation probability: {deviation_frequency:.3f}")
print(f"CLT approximation: {2 * stats.norm.sf(2):.3f}")
print("Chebyshev upper bound: 0.250")







Figure 6: Sampling distributions of standardized empirical averages from an Exponential(1) population. Dashed curves show the standard Normal density. The fourth empirical moment remains strongly non-Normal at n=40.





Simulated deviation probability: 0.044
CLT approximation: 0.046
Chebyshev upper bound: 0.250


What do we observe?

The standardized sample mean increasingly resembles a standard Normal distribution as \(n\) grows.
At the same sample size, the fourth empirical moment has a much more asymmetric sampling distribution.
The CLT-based probability approximation is substantially more informative than the Markov upper bound for the sample mean in this example.

The CLT therefore complements the LLN: convergence alone does not tell us how reliable a finite-sample estimate is. The variance determines its standard-error scale, while the CLT provides an approximate distribution for the standardized error.






WarningAn important limitation: infinite variance



The standard i.i.d. CLT requires finite variance. For a Cauchy distribution, even the population mean is undefined. The average of i.i.d. Cauchy observations remains Cauchy-distributed, regardless of the sample size. Neither the finite-mean LLN nor the standard CLT applies in this case. Note, however, that infinite variance alone does not invalidate the LLN if the absolute first moment is finite.

section: 5.3 Frequentist interpretation: Conditional expectation and prediction errors
text:
5.3 Frequentist interpretation: Conditional expectation and prediction errors
We have seen that the conditional expectation \(m(X)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X]\) minimizes the population mean squared prediction error:
\[
R(g)=\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2].
\]
But in statistical applications, we do not observe the population distribution. Instead, we observe a random sample
\[
(X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_n,Y_n).
\]
This suggests estimating the population prediction error by the empirical mean squared error:
\[
\widehat R_n(g)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-g(X_i))^2.
\]
If the observations are i.i.d. and the population prediction error is finite, the strong law of large numbers gives
\[
\boxed{
\widehat R_n(g)
\xrightarrow{a.s.}
R(g).
}
\]
Thus, the empirical average of squared prediction errors approaches the expected squared prediction error as the sample size increases.
This provides a frequentist interpretation of conditional expectation: Among all prediction functions, the conditional expectation achieves the smallest expected squared error, and repeated observations allow us to approximate these expected errors by empirical averages.

5.3.1 Example: Comparing three predictors
Suppose that
\[
X\sim N(0,1),\qquad
Y=X^2+\varepsilon,
\qquad
\varepsilon\sim N(0,1),
\]
where \(X\) and \(\varepsilon\) are independent.
Since \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X]=0\),
\[
m(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=x^2.
\]
We compare three candidate predictors:
\[
g_1(x)=1,\qquad
g_2(x)=x,\qquad
g_3(x)=x^2.
\]
Their population mean squared errors are
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(g_1)&=\mathbb E[(Y-1)^2]=3,\\
R(g_2)&=\mathbb E[(Y-X)^2]=5,\\
R(g_3)&=\mathbb E[(Y-X^2)^2]=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last predictor is the conditional expectation. It minimizes the mean squared prediction error.
Indeed, for every square-integrable prediction function \(g\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(g)
&=\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2]\\
&=\underbrace{\mathbb E[\varepsilon^2]}_{=1}
+\mathbb E[(X^2-g(X))^2]\\
&\geq 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The excess prediction error is therefore
\[
\boxed{
R(g)-R(m)=\mathbb E[(m(X)-g(X))^2].
}
\]


5.3.2 Visualizing the predictors and the data
We simulate observations from the joint distribution of \((X,Y)\) and compare the three prediction functions in a single graph.

rng_pred = np.random.default_rng(2029)

n = 500
x = rng_pred.normal(size=n)
epsilon = rng_pred.normal(size=n)
y = x**2 + epsilon

grid = np.linspace(-3, 3, 400)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

# Observed data
ax.scatter(
    x, y,
    color="gray",
    alpha=0.3,
    s=18,
    label="Observed data"
)

# Three prediction functions
ax.plot(
    grid, np.ones_like(grid),
    color="tab:green", ls="--", lw=2.5,
    label=r"$g_1(x)=1$"
)

ax.plot(
    grid, grid,
    color="tab:orange", ls="--", lw=2.5,
    label=r"$g_2(x)=x$"
)

ax.plot(
    grid, grid**2,
    color="tab:blue", lw=3,
    label=r"$g_3(x)=x^2=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$"
)

ax.set_xlabel("X")
ax.set_ylabel("Y")
ax.set_title("Conditional expectation and prediction")
ax.set_xlim(-3, 3)
ax.set_ylim(-4, 11)
ax.legend()

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Compare empirical and theoretical prediction errors
predictions = {
    "Constant (1)": (np.ones_like(x), 3),
    "Linear (x)": (x, 5),
    "Conditional mean (x²)": (x**2, 1)
}

print("Predictor                 Empirical MSE   Population MSE")
print("-" * 60)

for name, (prediction, theoretical_mse) in predictions.items():
    empirical_mse = np.mean((y - prediction)**2)
    print(f"{name:27s} {empirical_mse:10.3f} {theoretical_mse:14.3f}")







Figure 7: Observed data and three prediction functions. The conditional expectation x² minimizes the population mean squared prediction error.





Predictor                 Empirical MSE   Population MSE
------------------------------------------------------------
Constant (1)                     2.792          3.000
Linear (x)                       4.097          5.000
Conditional mean (x²)            1.054          1.000


What do we observe?

The observations fluctuate around the conditional expectation \(m(x)=x^2\) because of the random noise \(\varepsilon\).
The constant predictor \(g_1(x)=1\) uses no information about \(X\).
The predictor \(g_2(x)=x\) uses \(X\), but does not capture the nonlinear relationship.
The conditional expectation \(g_3(x)=x^2\) has the smallest expected squared prediction error.

The empirical MSEs differ from the theoretical values because we observe only a finite sample. By the LLN, these differences vanish as the sample size increases.
Interestingly, in this example,
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.
\]
Thus, \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated, even though knowing \(X\) is extremely useful for predicting \(Y\).
In fact, the best affine linear predictor of \(Y\) from \(X\) is the constant function \(1\), not the candidate \(g_2(x)=x\).






ImportantKey takeaway



The conditional expectation minimizes the population mean squared prediction error.
The law of large numbers allows us to approximate population prediction errors by empirical averages:
\[
\underbrace{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-g(X_i))^2}_{\text{Empirical prediction error}}
\xrightarrow{a.s.}
\underbrace{\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2]}_{\text{Population prediction error}}.
\]
The central limit theorem can additionally describe the sampling uncertainty of these empirical prediction errors, provided their variances are finite and positive.

title: 1. Random Variables, Distributions, and Limits
section: 3.3 Frequentist interpretation: Prediction and mean squared error
text:
3.3 Frequentist interpretation: Prediction and mean squared error
We have seen that the conditional expectation
\[
m(X)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X]
\]
is the best predictor of \(Y\) based on \(X\) when prediction errors are measured by mean squared error.
However, in statistics, we often restrict ourselves to a particular class of prediction functions.
For example, the best linear predictor (allowing an intercept) is defined by
\[
\boxed{
g^*_{\mathrm{lin}}
\in
\underset{g(x)=a+bx}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2].
}
\]
The conditional expectation, in contrast, minimizes the population mean squared error over all square-integrable functions of \(X\):
\[
\boxed{
m
\in
\underset{g}{\operatorname{argmin}}
\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2].
}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-m(X))^2]
\leq
\mathbb E[(Y-g^*_{\mathrm{lin}}(X))^2].
\]
The inequality may be strict: Even the best linear predictor can be substantially worse than the conditional expectation if the relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\) is nonlinear.

3.3.1 Example: Best linear predictor vs. conditional expectation
Consider
\[
X\sim N(0,1),\qquad
Y=X^2+\varepsilon,
\qquad
\varepsilon\sim N(0,1),
\]
where \(X\) and \(\varepsilon\) are independent.
The conditional expectation is
\[
m(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]=x^2.
\]
Recall that the population-optimal affine predictor is
\[
g^*_{\mathrm{lin}}(x)
=
\mathbb E[Y]
+
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
(x-\mathbb E[X]).
\]
Since
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=1,\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0,
\]
we obtain
\[
\boxed{g^*_{\mathrm{lin}}(x)=1.}
\]
Thus, even the best affine predictor does not capture the nonlinear relationship.
The population prediction errors are
\[
\begin{aligned}
R(g^*_{\mathrm{lin}})
&=\mathbb E[(Y-1)^2]=3,\\
R(m)
&=\mathbb E[(Y-X^2)^2]=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
We visualize the observations and both population-optimal prediction functions.

rng_pred = np.random.default_rng(2029)

n = 500
x = rng_pred.normal(size=n)
epsilon = rng_pred.normal(size=n)
y = x**2 + epsilon

grid = np.linspace(-3, 3, 400)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))

ax.scatter(
    x, y,
    color="gray", alpha=0.3, s=18,
    label="Observed data"
)

ax.plot(
    grid, np.ones_like(grid),
    color="tab:orange", ls="--", lw=2.5,
    label=r"Best affine predictor: $g^*_{\mathrm{lin}}(x)=1$"
)

ax.plot(
    grid, grid**2,
    color="tab:blue", lw=3,
    label=r"Conditional expectation: $m(x)=x^2$"
)

ax.set_xlabel("X")
ax.set_ylabel("Y")
ax.set_title("Best linear prediction vs. conditional expectation")
ax.set_xlim(-3, 3)
ax.set_ylim(-4, 11)
ax.legend()

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("Predictor                 Empirical MSE   Population MSE")
print("-" * 60)

for name, prediction, theoretical in [
    ("Best affine predictor", np.ones(n), 3),
    ("Conditional expectation", x**2, 1)
]:
    empirical = np.mean((y - prediction)**2)
    print(f"{name:27s} {empirical:10.3f} {theoretical:14.3f}")







Figure 7: Best affine predictor versus conditional expectation. Although the optimal affine predictor is constant, the conditional expectation captures the nonlinear relationship.





Predictor                 Empirical MSE   Population MSE
------------------------------------------------------------
Best affine predictor            2.792          3.000
Conditional expectation          1.054          1.000


What do we observe?
The conditional expectation has a smaller mean squared prediction error, even though the affine predictor is already optimal within its own function class.
This does not mean that conditional expectations are necessarily nonlinear. For example, if
\[
Y=2+3X+\varepsilon,
\qquad \mathbb E[\varepsilon\mid X]=0,
\]
then
\[
m(x)=2+3x.
\]
In that case, the best affine predictor and the conditional expectation coincide.
The important distinction is therefore not linear versus nonlinear prediction, but optimization over a restricted function class versus optimization over all admissible prediction functions.

title: 1. Random Variables, Distributions, and Limits
section: 3.4 Frequentist interpretation: Conditional expectation and prediction
text:
3.4 Frequentist interpretation: Conditional expectation and prediction
We have seen that the conditional expectation \[
m(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]
\] minimizes the population mean squared prediction error \[
R(g)=\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2].
\] But what does this mean in terms of observable prediction errors?
Suppose we observe a random sample \[
(X_1,Y_1),\ldots,(X_n,Y_n).
\] Since we cannot directly observe the population expectation, we might try to replace it by an empirical average: \[
\widehat R_n(g)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-g(X_i))^2.
\] It seems natural to find the prediction function that minimizes this empirical criterion: \[
\widehat g
\in
\underset{g}{\operatorname{argmin}}\;
\widehat R_n(g).
\]
But there is a problem. If we allow arbitrary prediction functions and the observed covariate values are distinct, we can always construct a function satisfying \[
\widehat g(X_i)=Y_i
\qquad\text{for all }i=1,\ldots,n.
\] Such a function interpolates all observations and therefore achieves \[
\boxed{\widehat R_n(\widehat g)=0.}
\] Does this mean we have found a perfect predictor? No. The function may simply reproduce the observed data without predicting new observations accurately. This phenomenon is called overfitting.
Consider again \[
X\sim N(0,1),\qquad
Y=X^2+\varepsilon,\qquad
\varepsilon\sim N(0,1),
\] where \(X\) and \(\varepsilon\) are independent. The conditional expectation is \[
m(x)=x^2,
\] with population mean squared prediction error \[
R(m)=\mathbb E[\varepsilon^2]=1.
\] The best affine predictor is the constant function \[
g^*_{\mathrm{lin}}(x)=1,
\] with population mean squared prediction error \[
R(g^*_{\mathrm{lin}})=3.
\]
We now construct a third predictor by connecting the observed data points with straight lines. This interpolating function achieves zero empirical prediction error on the original observations. But what happens when we use these prediction functions on new, independently generated observations?

rng_pred = np.random.default_rng(2029)

# -----------------------------------------
# 1. Initial observations
# -----------------------------------------

n_initial = 20

x_initial = rng_pred.normal(size=n_initial)
y_initial = x_initial**2 + rng_pred.normal(size=n_initial)

# Construct a piecewise linear interpolating function
order = np.argsort(x_initial)

x_sorted = x_initial[order]
y_sorted = y_initial[order]

def interpolator(x):
    return np.interp(x, x_sorted, y_sorted)

def best_affine(x):
    return np.ones_like(x)

def conditional_mean(x):
    return x**2

print("Empirical MSE on original observations:")
for name, g in [
    ("Interpolator", interpolator),
    ("Best affine predictor", best_affine),
    ("Conditional expectation", conditional_mean)
]:
    mse = np.mean((y_initial - g(x_initial))**2)
    print(f"{name:28s}: {mse:.4f}")

# -----------------------------------------
# 2. Independent repetitions
# -----------------------------------------

R = 3000
batch_size = 20

# Every repetition generates new X and Y values
x_new = rng_pred.normal(size=(R, batch_size))
y_new = x_new**2 + rng_pred.normal(size=(R, batch_size))

predictors = {
    "Interpolator": interpolator,
    "Best affine predictor": best_affine,
    "Conditional expectation": conditional_mean
}

repetitions = np.arange(1, R + 1)
running_errors = {}

for name, g in predictors.items():

    # Mean squared error in each new experiment
    mse_rep = np.mean((y_new - g(x_new))**2, axis=1)

    # Average across independent repetitions
    running_errors[name] = np.cumsum(mse_rep) / repetitions

# -----------------------------------------
# 3. Visualization
# -----------------------------------------

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))

grid = np.linspace(-3, 3, 400)

colors = {
    "Interpolator": "tab:green",
    "Best affine predictor": "tab:orange",
    "Conditional expectation": "tab:blue"
}

# Left: Observations and predictors
axes[0].scatter(
    x_initial, y_initial,
    color="black", s=24, alpha=0.7,
    label="Observed data", zorder=5
)

for name, g in predictors.items():
    axes[0].plot(
        grid, g(grid),
        lw=2,
        color=colors[name],
        label=name
    )

axes[0].set_xlabel("X")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Y")
axes[0].set_title("Fitting the observed data")
axes[0].set_xlim(-3, 3)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)

# Right: Errors in repeated new experiments
for name, errors in running_errors.items():
    axes[1].plot(
        repetitions, errors,
        color=colors[name],
        lw=1.7,
        label=name
    )

# Known population MSEs
axes[1].axhline(
    3, color="tab:orange", ls="--", alpha=0.6
)
axes[1].axhline(
    1, color="tab:blue", ls="--", alpha=0.6
)

axes[1].set_xscale("log")
axes[1].set_xlim(10, R)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Number of independent repetitions")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Average squared prediction error")
axes[1].set_title("Predicting new observations")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Empirical MSE on original observations:
Interpolator                : 0.0000
Best affine predictor       : 1.1414
Conditional expectation     : 1.1163








Figure 8: Left: An interpolating predictor fits the observed data exactly, while the conditional expectation captures the underlying relationship. Right: Average prediction errors across new independent experiments.





What do we observe?

The interpolating function achieves zero empirical MSE on the original observations.
Nevertheless, its prediction errors on new observations are not zero.
As the number of independent repetitions increases, the average squared prediction errors stabilize.
The conditional expectation achieves the smallest long-run average squared prediction error.

This reveals an important distinction: A function that perfectly describes observed data need not be a good predictor of new observations.

To understand the predictive interpretation of conditional expectation, consider the following random experiment for a fixed prediction function \(g\):

Draw a new pair \((X,Y)\) from the population.
Predict \(Y\) using \(g(X)\).
Calculate the squared prediction error \((Y-g(X))^2\).

We repeat this experiment independently \(N\) times, keeping the prediction function \(g\) unchanged.
The average squared prediction error is
\[
\widehat R_N(g)
=
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(Y_i-g(X_i))^2.
\]
By the strong law of large numbers, for every fixed \(g\) with finite mean squared prediction error,
\[
\boxed{
\widehat R_N(g)
\xrightarrow{a.s.}
\mathbb E[(Y-g(X))^2].
}
\]
Thus, the expected squared prediction error is the long-run average squared prediction error when we repeatedly use the same function to predict new observations.
Recall that we have already established that the conditional expectation
\[
m(x)=\mathbb E[Y\mid X=x]
\]
minimizes the population mean squared prediction error over all admissible prediction functions.
The law of large numbers therefore provides the following frequentist interpretation: The conditional expectation is the prediction function that minimizes the long-run average squared prediction error when predicting new independent observations.






ImportantFrequentist interpretation of conditional expectation



Importantly, this does not mean that it minimizes the prediction error on every particular sample. A function may achieve zero error on the observations used to construct it, while performing poorly on new observations. This is the problem of overfitting.

1.5 Expectation, variance, covariance, and moments
The expected value of \(X\), when it exists, is its probability-weighted average:
\[
\mathbb E[X]=\begin{cases}
\sum_x x\,p_X(x),&X\text{ discrete},\\[3pt]

\end{cases}
\]

\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\mathbb E[X]+b\mathbb E[Y]
\] without requiring independence.
Writing \(\mu=\mathbb E[X]\), the variance and standard deviation are \[
\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)^2]
=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mu^2,\qquad
\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
\]
A raw moment is \(\mathbb E[X^k]\); a central moment is \(\mathbb E[(X-\mu)^k]\). The second central moment is the variance. Higher moments can describe aspects of distributional shape, provided they exist.
For two random variables, \[
\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])],
\] and, when both standard deviations are positive, \(\operatorname{Corr}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/(\operatorname{SD}(X)\operatorname{SD}(Y))\).
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)
+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y).
\] When \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)= 0\), this is Bienyamé’s formula. Independence implies zero covariance (when the relevant moments exist); the converse is generally false.
Like probabilities, moments can also be interpreted in a frequentist context: They are the (scaling) limits of sums of independent random experiments. That is, \[\mathbb E[X^m]= \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac 1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^m\]$ with probability \(1\) when \(\mathbb E[|X|^m]<\infty\) and \(X_1,...,X_n\) are independent random variables with the same distribution as \(X\). This frequentist interpretation is a direct corollary of the law of large numbers. We will discuss it in the next section
